query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In compositionally complex, single‐phase HEAs, high-strain sliding in an ultra-high vacuum environment dynamically refines the coarse grain structure to a nanoscale regime (approaching critical grain sizes of roughly 10–50 nm), triggering a transition from dislocation-driven plasticity to grain boundary–dominated deformation (e.g., grain-boundary sliding and incipient cavitation) that results in brittle behavior—even in the absence of impurity-induced embrittlement typical in conventional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: An additively manufactured, single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) with a coarse-grained microstructure and high ductility.
generation.intervention: Controlled high-strain sliding tests conducted in UHV with systematic variation of strain rate and temperature.
generation.conditions: Tests performed in an ultra-high vacuum to avoid oxidation and impurity segregation; temperature and strain rate ranges chosen to induce dynamic grain refinement without thermally-activated phase separation (e.g., intermediate temperatures and high strain rates).
generation.structural_mediator: Dynamic grain refinement leading to a nanocrystalline surface layer (grain sizes approaching 10–50 nm).
generation.mechanism: The extreme shear imposed during sliding leads to rapid grain size reduction. As the grains reach a critical size, the dominant deformation mechanism shifts from dislocation slip to grain boundary sliding and cavitation-like failure modes, promoting brittle behavior. This is distinct from conventional alloys, where embrittlement is driven by impurity segregation and grain-boundary precipitation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under the testing conditions, the HEA is expected to initially exhibit ductile behavior but then experience a sudden drop in ductility accompanied by increased friction (or altered wear patterns) and the appearance of brittle fracture features (e.g., cavitation along grain boundaries) once the surface grains are refined to the critical nanoscale size. By contrast, conventional alloys would require impurity-driven grain-boundary weakening to exhibit such a brittle response.
generation.baseline: The as-manufactured, coarse-grained HEA displays high ductility and non-brittle behavior under moderate sliding conditions, with deformation dominated by dislocation mechanisms.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to conditions where the temperature and strain rate are sufficient to induce rapid grain refinement but are below thresholds that trigger significant impurity segregation or phase transformation. It may not hold at very high temperatures or very low strain rates where the refinement mechanism is either overridden by thermal processes or insufficiently activated.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical grain size threshold for the ductile-to-brittle transition and the relative contributions of grain-boundary sliding versus decohesion or cavitation in causing brittle failure remain to be quantitatively determined. In addition, while UHV conditions minimize impurity effects, subtle segregation effects at high strains cannot be entirely ruled out.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of additively manufactured single-phase HEA specimens and subject them to high-strain sliding tests in UHV while systematically varying strain rate and temperature. Simultaneously, carry out identical tests on a conventional alloy known to undergo impurity-driven embrittlement. Characterize the surface microstructure evolution in situ (or ex situ immediately after testing) using transmission electron microscopy and fractography, and correlate the grain size with the mechanical performance (ductility, friction coefficient, and wear rate).
measurements: Grain size distribution via TEM after various strain and temperature conditions
Mechanical response (stress-strain curves, ductility, fracture toughness)
Friction coefficient and wear-rate measurements during sliding
Surface fractography to detect signs of grain-boundary cavitation or decohesion
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA does not exhibit a significant transition from ductile to brittle behavior correlated with a critical nanoscale grain size (i.e., no abrupt loss in ductility or onset of brittle fracture features) under high-strain sliding in UHV, or if similar behavior is observed in both the HEA and the conventional alloy (implying impurity-driven embrittlement governs the response), the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Since their discovery in 2004,, high entropy alloys (HEAs) have been extensively investigated and shown to exhibit remarkable thermomechanical properties,. Studies of grain-size dependent mechanical behavior are limited,, however, especially in the regime of ultra-nanocrystalline grain size where softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) occurs. Recent work has also shown that these alloys are ideally suited for processing using laser-based additive manufacturing techniques, as they exhibit high phase stability and derive much of their strength from thermal history-insensitive mechanisms like solution strengthening. While recent publications have presented experimental evidence of low friction or high wear resistance (but typically not both) with HEAs, they were performed in environments where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide surface films was prevalent. These phenomena can greatly impact strength and deformation/wear resistance. The Hall-Petch equation, σy=σ0+k⋅d−1/2, is fit to the Luo data only, and agrees reasonably well with the nano-grained estimate from Schuh, et al.. Recent work has shown that low friction of bare metals, in the range μ≅0.2−0.5, can be explained as the dynamic softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) of surfaces due to highly surface-localized, shear-induced severe plastic deformation,,. This is well described by a recently proposed predictive model that explains the low shear strength and friction coefficients of bare metals and alloys. This model of grain size-dependent shear strength requires no fitting parameters and is based exclusively on materials properties and physically meaningful input parameters like temperature and shear rate. Although recent experimental measurements of HAGB energy with this same alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) exist, a comparison of this prediction is difficult. Measurements of grain boundary energy are sensitive to thermally-driven grain boundary segregation (and possibly phase separation) of impurities. This value is relatively high for metals,, and may imply a propensity for localized cohesive failure or fracture at the boundaries. Grain boundary decohesion has been recently shown to occur readily for this alloy due to segregation and nanoclustering of Cr, Ni and Mn at elevated temperature, and these failures typically originate along HAGBs and at triple junctions. In the present work there is no significant evidence of grain boundary segregation, and this is reasonable as a negligible increase in temperature is expected for these sliding conditions. This suggests that this alloy may also be prone to grain boundary decohesion without significant segregation and phase separation, i.e., when it is a solid solution. reading.lever: Conduct controlled high-strain sliding tests in UHV, systematically varying strain rate and temperature to trigger and track grain refinement and brittle transition.
reading.why: This approach builds on evidence of dynamic grain refinement causing inverse Hall–Petch behavior in HEAs, offering a direct test against conventional impurity-driven embrittlement.
